Unlimited power.

The technological progress made by our civilization during the last 10 years is mind-blowing.

The sheer pace is extraordinary. The steam engine transformed the eighteenth century. Electricity reshaped the nineteenth. Mass production defined the twentieth. The internet revolutionized the late twentieth and early twenty-first.

The last ten years compressed several such revolutions into a single decade. If someone from 2015 were suddenly dropped into 2026, they would recognize the world—but they would constantly stumble upon things that simply did not exist.

In barely a decade, artificial intelligence went from amusing image classifiers to systems that can write software, conduct research, translate dozens of languages, generate films, compose music, analyze medical scans, tutor students, and reason across text, images, audio, and video—all from a device that fits in a pocket.

We made reusable orbital rockets routine. We began catching boosters in mid-air, launched tens of thousands of satellites into low Earth orbit, and turned continuous global broadband from orbit into a commercial reality. Private companies now accomplish feats that once required Cold War superpowers.

Gene editing left the laboratory and entered medicine. CRISPR-based therapies are treating diseases once considered lifelong genetic sentences. mRNA technology proved it could be designed, manufactured, and deployed at unprecedented speed, opening an entirely new pharmaceutical platform.

Robots learned to see, manipulate objects, and navigate human environments. Humanoid machines are beginning to work in factories. 

Autonomous vehicles now operate commercial taxi services in several cities without human drivers.

Renewable energy became the cheapest source of new electricity across much of the world. Battery costs collapsed, electric vehicles became mass-market products, and grid-scale energy storage moved from demonstration projects to industrial deployment.

Quantum computing crossed from theoretical promise to machines capable of solving increasingly sophisticated experimental problems.

Fusion research achieved ignition, something generations of physicists pursued without success.

The smartphone became a universal tool: camera, television studio, map, bank, translator, passport, office, shopping center, encyclopedia, and increasingly, an AI assistant that would have seemed indistinguishable from science fiction only a few years ago.

The next ten years are unlikely to be slower. They will probably bring general-purpose robots into homes and factories, AI systems capable of carrying out weeks of intellectual work in hours, personalized medicine based on an individual's genome, fully autonomous transport on a much larger scale, abundant clean electricity from ever-cheaper solar, wind, batteries and perhaps early fusion, routine manufacturing in orbit, and a permanent human presence beyond Earth. If the last decade taught us anything, it is that technological progress is no longer advancing at a steady pace—it is accelerating. 

The greatest surprise of 2036 may well be how much of today's science fiction has become so ordinary that people no longer think about it.

There is a specific kind of frustration that comes from building something with Claude Code, Codex, or Lovable, getting it working exactly how you wanted and then hitting a wall when you try to share it with someone.
You cannot just send them your laptop 😂😂.

Deployment is where a lot of momentum dies for PMs and builders. Not because it is impossibly hard, but because nobody ever walked them through what actually happens between your local machine and a live URL that someone else can open.
That gap is exactly what this session is closing.
Mayowa Tudonu — Blockchain Engineer and Solutions Architect at Chainlink Labs, with experience building production systems at Jumia Nigeria, Interswitch Group, and Buycoins, is taking an AI-built application from local to live in real time. On screen. No slides about what is possible. Just the actual process.

You will leave knowing which deployment platform suits what you built, why something that worked on your machine sometimes breaks when it goes live, and what the most common first-time deployment mistakes are before they happen to you.

A first-of-its-kind open-source video generation model for embodied scenarios, using a Mixture-of-Experts design. 

LingBot-Video from @robbyant_brain, a Diffusion Transformer video foundation model built for embodied AI.

- The flagship 30B model activates only 3B parameters per generation, at 1M-token sequences

- At the same total parameter scale it reaches ~3X the inference efficiency of a Dense architecture at 1M-token sequences (3.18× vs. Dense 30B)

- Aesthetic-only reward models are why video generators fake physics, and this paper basically says so. Physical plausibility is not treated as vibes here; it gets scored through causality, object permanence, non-penetration and material realism.

- The model was not trained only on regular internet videos. Its pretraining data also includes 70,000+ hours of embodied footage, covering robot manipulation, navigation, and first-person action videos, so the model sees examples where movement actually changes the world.

- On RBench, it reports a 0.620 average, ahead of every listed open and closed model, while still losing some columns to Wan 2.6.
